name: Diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate
lead: Diethylamino hydroxybenzoyl hexyl benzoate (DHHB), sold as Uvinul A Plus (BASF) and Parsol DHHB (DSM), is an oil-soluble organic UVA filter with an absorption maximum near 354 nm, noted for photostability and compatibility with other UV absorbers.[1][2]

The EU approved it for sunscreens in 2005 at up to 10%, and it is also approved in several other markets including Japan; in the US, Wikipedia says it may be used for product protection rather than as a sunscreen active.[1]

Published work on DHHB specifically covers laboratory photochemistry, formulation, human metabolism and excretion, safety assessment, and environmental monitoring.[3][4][9][10][11] A notable regulatory discussion concerns a manufacturing contaminant, di-n-hexyl phthalate.[1] A 2026 risk assessment calculated a wide margin of safety for typical sunscreen use, and a 2020 human study followed how volunteers metabolise and excrete it.[12][9]

paras: DHHB is made by reacting 3-hydroxy-N,N-diethylaniline with phthalic anhydride and esterifying the product with 1-hexanol.[1] It is used in sunscreens and SPF cosmetics, often with UVB filters, and studies of filter-filter interactions examine how filters photostabilise one another and quench excited states.[3] Formulation research has tested it in nanostructured lipid carriers and nanoemulsions for photostability and skin penetration,[4] and in sprayable emulsions.[5]
A US drug label lists it, alongside ethylhexyl triazone, bisoctrizole and diethylhexyl butamido triazone, in a sunscreen product.[6]

Ultraviolet A (320 to 400 nm) penetrates deeper than UVB and is associated with photoaging, which is why UVA filters are a core part of broad-spectrum sunscreens aimed at preventing wrinkles and uneven tone as well as sunburn.[2] DHHB absorbs strongly across that range with a peak at 354 nm and dissipates the energy as heat rather than breaking down, a property Grokipedia contrasts with avobenzone, which can lose efficacy in sunlight.[2] A 2017 photophysics study found that DHHB loses its excited-state energy through a rapid intramolecular proton transfer, and that its triplet energy is higher than those of octyl methoxycinnamate and octocrylene, so it may transfer energy to those UVB filters in mixtures.[10] A 2023 study of DHHB nanoparticles stabilised with a surfactant found that they kept the same fast excited-state relaxation while becoming easier to disperse in water.[11]

The US drug label for one sunscreen lists DHHB together with ethylhexyl triazone, bisoctrizole and diethylhexyl butamido triazone, and states that the product helps prevent sunburn and, used as directed with other sun protection, decreases the risk of skin cancer and early skin aging.[6] The US FDA has not listed DHHB among its permitted sunscreen actives, and Grokipedia reports that Canada also does not permit it.[1][2]

Studies of filter-filter interactions examine how pairs of filters stabilise each other and quench excited states and singlet oxygen.[3] Grokipedia describes DHHB as pairing with octocrylene to extend UVA-plus-UVB coverage.[2]

In a human study, volunteers received a single oral or dermal dose of DHHB and urine was collected for 72 hours. Three major urinary metabolites accounted for 52 percent of the oral dose, with four minor metabolites carrying an additional hydroxyl group, and the authors used the conversion factors to estimate exposure in 58 volunteers not intentionally exposed.[9] Grokipedia cites animal data suggesting percutaneous absorption of roughly 0.04 to 0.10 percent.[2]

DHHB is a benzophenone derivative (C24H31NO4, 397.5 g/mol) with a diethylamino and a hydroxy group on one ring and a hexyl ester on the other, which makes it oil-soluble and very poorly soluble in water.[1][2] It is marketed as Uvinul A Plus by BASF and as Parsol DHHB by DSM.[1] The EU approved it for sunscreens in 2005, and the maximum permitted concentration is 10 percent in the EU, with other approving markets including Japan, China and Australia.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes DHHB as a safe sunscreen ingredient, with the main concern being the contaminant di-n-hexyl phthalate, which the European Chemicals Agency listed as a Substance of Very High Concern in 2013.[1] The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety recommended a maximum of 260 ppm of this contaminant, with a target below 1 ppm because the contamination is avoidable.[1] Grokipedia cites the SCCS as confirming safety up to 10% with impurities controlled, and reports minimal percutaneous absorption in animal models.[2]

A 2026 risk assessment of DHHB as a cosmetic ingredient reported low acute toxicity, no evidence of genotoxicity and minimal skin irritation or sensitisation. Using a no-observed-adverse-effect level of 200 mg/kg body weight per day from a rat reproductive study, daily use of 17 g of a 10 percent product and 0.15 percent dermal absorption, it estimated a systemic exposure of 0.0425 mg/kg per day and a margin of safety of 4,705, above the threshold of 100 normally applied.[12] European human-biomonitoring partnerships (PARC and HBM4EU) have derived a health-based guidance value for DHHB in biological samples, the concentration below which no adverse effects are expected from exposure to the substance alone.[13]

Eight UV filters, a group that included DHHB, were measured on Gran Canaria beaches in a 2015 environmental risk assessment,[7] and DHHB was among ten filters tested on brine shrimp and marine microalgae.[8]

A 2023 study of swimming pools found that free chlorine drove about 85 percent of DHHB degradation under chlorine and sunlight, forming seven transformation by-products, and that degradation was slowed in tap-water pools and faster in seawater pools.[14] A 2025 study made a glucuronide metabolite of DHHB, which occurs as a human phase II metabolite, and tested its toxicity to aquatic organisms.[15]
Grokipedia reports that DHHB reacts with chlorine bleach to form red compounds, and that seven of eleven commercial sunscreens containing it left crimson stains on fabric when later bleached.[2]

No clinical trial of sunscreen efficacy for DHHB alone was found. The human data are a toxicokinetic study in volunteers, in which a single oral or dermal dose was followed by urine analysis,[9] and biomonitoring guidance values derived from such data.[13] A 2026 risk assessment relies on animal toxicity data and exposure modelling.[12] Related laboratory research covers photochemistry, formulation, and environmental fate.[3][4][5][10][11][14]

timeline.event: EU approves DHHB for sunscreens at up to 10%.[1]

card.summary: A photostable UVA sunscreen filter common outside the US; evidence is lab-based and regulatory.
card.aka: DHHB, Uvinul A Plus, Parsol DHHB
card.note: Not a US sunscreen active; EU advisers set limits on a phthalate contaminant.

quick.overview:
DHHB is an oil-soluble sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVA light. It is photostable and used in products in the EU, Japan and other markets.

It is not a US-approved sunscreen active, and no clinical trials of it alone were found.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVA near 354 nm and dissipates the energy, and studies show it interacts with other filters to help stabilise them.
quick.risks: The main regulatory concern is a manufacturing contaminant, di-n-hexyl phthalate, for which EU advisers recommended strict limits. Environmental monitoring studies have detected UV filters on beaches.

chain: Absorbs UVA light (320-400 nm) on the skin
Less UVA reaches the skin, which drives photoaging and pigmentation
Skin keeps a more even tone and fewer sun-related wrinkles over time
angle.text: DHHB is a sunscreen ingredient that absorbs UVA, the part of sunlight associated with skin aging, wrinkles and uneven pigmentation. People using sunscreens that contain it are using a UVA filter that stays stable in sunlight and can be paired with UVB filters in one product, which is how it fits into routines aimed at keeping skin looking younger.
